sections.html:
• Other names: Red Fire shrimp, Fire shrimp, Blood shrimp, Cardinal cleaner shrimp, Scarlet cleaner shrimp, Taiwan Fire Red shrimp
  • Minimum tank size: 60 litres
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Water type: SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Life span: up to 3 years
  • Colour: deep red with white dots
Red Fire shrimp are native to Sri Lanka, Bali (Indonesia) and Philippine waters, where they live in deep water (10–28 m). The species was described in 1983 and named after Helmut Debelius.

Because of their size and territorial behaviour, the minimum tank size for one shrimp is 60 litres. Larger tanks with large reef structures are preferable. If you keep a pair that do not get along, even a 110-litre tank may be too small.

This is a saltwater species (SG 1.023–1.025). Keep pH at 8.1–8.4 and temperature at 25–28°C. They are sensitive to ammonia and nitrite, so the tank must be fully cycled before introducing them, and the shrimp must be acclimated.
They prefer subdued lighting. Being shy, they need a rock structure or similar shelter to retreat to.

Their feeding is easy because they eat a variety of foods. They eat the scales and skin they clean from other fish. They also accept live or frozen copepods, pellets, flakes and other fish foods. As long as the other fish are fed, there is no need to target-feed the shrimp.

Red Fire shrimp are shy and nocturnal, so they are seldom seen during the day and tend to come out for food at night. With time they can get used to the keeper and come out more often in daytime.

They are known as cleaner shrimp because they pick dead scales and skin and remove ectoparasites from other fish. Many set up their own cleaning station. In the wild they associate with fishes, in particular groupers and giant moray eels (Gymnothorax spp.), in crevices between large boulders. Some reports say they can become lazy in captivity if given plenty of food.

They are normally found in pairs. They are territorial and can be quite aggressive towards their own kind; fights can end with lost limbs and antennae. Shrimp-on-shrimp aggression is not uncommon, so it is best to keep only one per tank.

They tend to get along with most other fish and shrimp, but large fish such as large flame cardinalfish will eat them whole. They are also incompatible with triggerfishes, puffers, larger hawkfish, larger wrasses, morays and lionfish. Some hobbyists report that they can pick at small polyps such as zoanthids and certain SPS corals, so expensive corals are best left out. Many individuals learn to recognise their keeper, come out to greet them and even eat from the hand.

There is no sexual dimorphism. They are simultaneous hermaphrodites: one individual has both female and male reproductive tissue and can act as either sex during a single spawning. At first all shrimp have only male organs and develop female organs as they mature. They cannot self-fertilise.

Any two individuals can be paired. According to studies, they become fully mature at a size of 2 cm.

Larval tank

  • Water temperature 28–30°C
  • Salinity 30–37 ppt
  • pH 7.7–8.5
  • Nitrate below 40 mg/L
  • Ammonia below 0.8 mg/L

A separate tank for the larvae is highly recommended. Do not use air stones or undergravel filtration, because larvae cannot control their movements and air stones often cause high larval mortality.

Spawning and development

The number of larvae per spawner varied from 600–1100 in one experiment and 1350–1900 in another, and increases with the weight of the parent. The female carries the eggs for the whole incubation (12–16 days depending on temperature) and releases larvae usually at night. The swimmerets of a shrimp carrying eggs appear darker than the abdominal segments above them.

Newly hatched zoea are strongly phototrophic and about 1–2 mm. They commonly swim telson first and upside-down. Within 2 days they moult to the 2nd larval stage (there are 6 stages), at 2–3 mm. By 7–8 days they reach 3–4 mm. Larvae turn into miniature adults 50–90 days after hatching, at an average length of 1 cm. In another experiment the larval period was 75–158 days. Survival was low, 9–18%.

Feeding larvae

Larvae need suitable food immediately after hatching. Without food in the first 6 hours they lose colour, swim less and may die within 24 hours, and later feeding usually cannot reverse the effects of early starvation.

  • Days 1–4: a mix of diatoms (Chaetoceros gracillis), Artemia nauplii, microalgae (Rhinomonas reticulata, Skeletonema costata, Tetraselmis chuii, Chlorella vulgaris), rotifers and Marine Cuisine. Microalgae alone are not enough to support growth or survival.
  • Days 5–12: add newly hatched Artemia nauplii enriched with Chlorella vulgaris.
  • From day 13 until metamorphosis: add pureed cuttlefish and live copepods at a density of 0.2 prey/mL.

Red Fire shrimp have a very deep, bright red colour with white dots on certain areas of the body, as well as white antennae and legs. They grow to 4–6 cm in length and usually live around 1.5–3 years.

Like all invertebrates, they need adequate calcium and trace minerals for moulting. When the shrimp moults, the exoskeleton should not be removed, because it contains calcium and other microelements and the shrimp will eat it later. Most experts recommend against adding iodine to the water.

The species is still mostly wild-caught: over 90% of traded specimens are collected from coral reefs, which has contributed to its endangered status. Captive breeding and larviculture protocols are being developed.
